utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today is Monday, the 9th of November, 2009. I would like to greet first and foremost the accused who are all present. I would like to greet all Defence counsel, as well as all the members of the OTP who are here today and all the people assisting us. I would like to give floor to the registrar who has got 3 IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Milan Gorjanc. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC1093, the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC1094, and finally the list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit IC1095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. I shall ask the usher to go and fetch our witness for today, Mr. Beneta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Can you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivan Beneta, the 14th of March, 1955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What is your current occupation? What do you actually do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an active officer with the rank of brigadier general, and I'm the assistant chief defence inspector in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, have you already testified before a Tribunal or is it the first time today that you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you read the text of the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. You may sit down. Just some information I'd like to convey to you. As you know, you will be asked to answer questions put to you by Ms. Alaburic. Ms. Alaburic is the Defence counsel of General Petkovic. At the end of that stage, the other counsel who represent the other accused may also put questions to you. The representatives of the OTP sitting to your right will also put questions to you as part of their cross-examination. The four Judges that make up the Bench and who are sitting before you may also put questions to you on the basis of documents we have before us. Please try and be as accurate as you possibly can when you answer the questions. If you don't understand a question, don't hesitate to ask the person putting question to you to rephrase it. In addition, you have just taken the solemn declaration, which means that you are now a witness of the court, and you may not contact anyone at all. Since your testimony is going to last several days, you should not meet up with anyone other than family members and avoid giving any interviews and avoid talking about what is happening in the courtroom. I would also like to add something else which I have not conveyed to witnesses so far because it seemed so obvious that I felt it wasn't necessary. Mr. Stewart mentioned something to the Judges which we have thought about. When a Judge puts you a question and you feel that the Judge is making a mistake when he is putting the question, if you don't agree with the way the question is put don't hesitate to tell the Judge, I don't agree. I believe you have made a mistake. It is not because a Judge makes a mistake that you should endorse what the Judge is saying. If, on the basis of the document, which says four vehicles, and the Judge says, "In this document three vehicles are mentioned," you should then say, "Sorry, Judge, but you've made a mistake. It says four and not three." Please do not hesitate, and I encourage you to intervene if necessary. So you may answer the questions freely and try and be as accurate as you possibly can when you provide those answers. If you were to feel uncomfortable during the hearing, you must let us know and we shall then stop the hearing. A hearing can be a very tiring experience, and some people sometimes feel uncomfortable in the course of it. If that is the case, please let us know and we shall then have a short break. This is what I wanted to share with you to make sure that this hearing unfolds in the best conditions possible. Ms. Alaburic, I would like to greet you once again and give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good day -- good afternoon to my learned friends from the OTP and from the other Defence teams. Good afternoon to you, General, and to everybody else assisting us today.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Beneta, we will first go into your biography, and then we will expand some periods of your life on some military issues that the Defence of General Petkovic considers relevant in these proceedings. You told us when you were born. Tell us where you were born too.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: I was born at Dubravica in the vicinity of Skradin, municipality of Sibenik in Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which country is that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will now read out some information about your education. You will please listen, and if I say anything wrong, please correct it, and if I say anything right, do confirm. You graduated from the military academy of the army, and you attended that academy for three years in Belgrade and one year in Zadar. You also reached the end of your studies of sociology on pedagogy, but you did not graduate from that faculty. After the war you completed the War College of the Croatian Army, courses for working in staffs organised by NATO. Furthermore, a school of management in the area of defence which was organised in England. And currently, you are completing your master's thesis at the Faculty of Political Science in Zagreb. The course of studies is entitled "European Union Law, Politics, and Economy." So law, politics, and economy, and you are writing a thesis entitled "The Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and the Transformation of that Country on the Path to the European Union." General, have I now correctly listed all the major steps in your education?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. All you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now a few words about your service. Until 1991, you served with the JNA in Zadar. At first you were at the secondary military school for seven years, after which you commanded a battery in the vicinity of Zadar, and in 1999 you were again teaching at the education -- sorry, the year was 1989, you taught at a training centre for reserve officer. Is that correct with regard to the beginning of your career?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes, but I also would like to stress the seven years that I spent at the secondary military school do not mean that I attended secondary military school for seven years. I was the headmaster of that school.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, General. Explain to us, please, this training centre for reserve officers. Who were these reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: That was a type of training developed through the concept of All People's Defence and social self-protection. The trainees were able-bodied men. Instead of serving their conscript service which was compulsory military service, they went through a shortened training course for soldiers where they acquired military schools and a rather demanding curriculum which enabled them to carry out the tasks of officers. They received their officer's rank once the territorial defence offices had appointed them to some unit, mostly a reserve unit, and once they had competed their first exercise with that unit, and then they would get their officer's rank [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, I would like to correct the transcript. On this page, in line 9, the word "officers" should have -- should also have had the attribute "reserve," so it should read "reserve officers."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, to somebody who is not from former Yugoslavia and to who the concept of All People's Defence is not familiar, how would you explain to that person the difference between an active officer and a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: An active officer is developed through his military career, and that is his main business for which he gets paid. A reserve officer goes through compulsory military service and after that lives as a civilian, but in accordance with the concept of All People's Defence and social self-protection, or, in other words, the concept of the armed people, apart from a job that he may hold with a company also goes to annual exercises, has his own unit, mostly reserve unit, that he prepares for warfare, and he is still liable to military service until the age of 65.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, if I understood you correctly, you said that after the reserve officers' school he goes to civilian life.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, due to this explanation, I would like to point out a mistake on page 6, line 22, where it reads that he lives as a civilian, but the witness is -- said that he lives a civilian life but remains a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, according to that concept of All People's Defence, able-bodied men, did they have duties towards the military, and if so, did only some of them have any such duty or all of them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Almost all men who are liable to military service or conscripts would have their personal register card, and the defence offices would post these conscripts with some units whether these were reserve units that would only be established in the framework of mobilisation, or they would complete the -- complete active units for wartime. There would also be a work obligation, especially in the case of subjects of special interest for the defence of the country, and that would be activated in the case -- in case of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, General, what was the principle criterion in deciding whether a particular individual would be assigned to a military unit or into civilian protection or into an enterprise or an institution to work as part of his work obligation? What was the main criterion for assignment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The principle criterion were his abilities, the best way to use that person with his particular knowledge and skills.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Last week we used the example of a chemistry engineer specialising in explosives, and if you were an employee of the military department, what would be your thoughts about where best to assign that chemistry engineer and explosives expert?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: He could be assigned as additional personnel, auxiliary personnel, in a logistical unit to be replenished in wartime. So he would continue as military personnel during the war. It would be a bonus if he completed an additional military school, but the very fact that he had served in the army would qualify him for service in a logistical unit. In addition, he could be engaged in an enterprise, in a factory that would produce explosives under a work obligation that could be imposed on the enterprise. If he is assigned that way, that would be his military obligation during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. I think we have clarified this concept of All People's Defence as applying to reserve officers sufficiently. I'd like to ask you about your work in the training -- secondary training centre in Zadar. Did Milivoj Petkovic also work at that centre at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Ms. Alaburic. I have one short question for you, Witness. The reserve officer that remains a conscript up to the age of 60, does this reserve officer increase in rank, and if he does what -- on the basis of what criteria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That officer is promoted up the hierarchy, and he rises in rank usually depending on military drills that he completes with his unit where he is usually one of the key people. These drills are held once or twice a year. And that kind of promotion would be a bit slower than with professional officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, General, I asked whether Milivoj Petkovic was working in some secondary training centre in Zadar at the same time.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petkovic worked in a neighbouring training centre that educated active and reserve officers in artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Petkovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We were not exactly friends, but I knew he was working there. I knew he was one of the officers employed at the training centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the quality of his work, his performance?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No, nothing in particular, but I also didn't hear of any problems connected to him and his duties. I think he was a successful officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you again about him later when we come to the Croatian Army. Let me now ask you about the relationship between the army and politics. In the Yugoslav People's Army was there an organised aspect of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav People's Army the only political party organisation in existence was the League of Communists. It was organised from grass-root level, from units up to the top military leadership in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of the 1990s, in all the republics of the former Yugoslavia other political parties come into existence, and the political authorities promote a multi-party system, and the first multi-party elections are prepared. What is happening at that time with the League of Communists inside the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The League of Communists remained, although time -- or the times were beginning to show that there was no reason for the status quo to be maintained, and certain absurd situation sometimes occurred on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what kind of absurd situations briefly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: There was not a clue about how to answer the question, "Are we going to continue admitting into military academies only people who were morally fit," as the term went, "loyal to the League of Communists?" And another question, since some serving soldiers were also part of these political organisations, what were we going to do if we get suddenly 20 soldiers who declare that they want to organise a Liberal Party inside the army?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was your position, General?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: At that time, towards the end of 1990, I was a member of the basic organisation of the League of Communists made up of teachers, instructors of the training centre. Sometime in November 1990, because of that situation that I just described I asked for our agenda at a meeting to include the self-abolishment of that party organisation so that we may set an example as to what needed to be done. Despite the opposition of the chief of that organisation --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It seems that the interpretation channels have been mixed up. It seems the -- it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: So in spite of the opposition of the chief of that organisation, the body of the staff voted that issue to be included in the agenda. And when the discussion came to that point, most of the younger staff, which formed the majority, voted that we abolish ourselves. Since it had been my proposal in the first place, I experienced later certain problems in the weeks and months that followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, about your position as a professional soldier. Is the army supposed to perform its duty and serve regardless of which political party is in power.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. I definitely believe that the army must have its own set of tasks and a mission that must be independent of political party aims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, in a well-organised society, who governs the army? Who manages the army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The army is governed by the head of state and in certain aspects the parliament and in yet other aspects the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your view, does the professional soldier have to be limitlessly, unrestrictedly obedient in following orders, or rather, after all, certain limits to obedience?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Despite the fact that soldiers are trained in the spirit of exceptional obedience, certain situations are described to them in their training where they have the right to refuse to obey.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Such as the commission of a crime and violations of the international laws of warfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, General. We'll continue through your biography. You joined the Croatian Army in July 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, about the position of the then Croatian president, Franjo Tudjman, concerning former JNA officers? Were they welcome into the Croatia army or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: I believe that in that very peculiar situation, just before the outbreak of the war and in the initial stages of the war, President Tudjman was quite aware of the need to include military personnel with skills and with experience in the war, and I believe he was seeking a certain balance between such men and other men who did not have that level of military knowledge but who in other terms seemed to be good choices for appointments in the army being established.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You, General, were first employed in the defence of Zadar. You were then employed in the defence of the hinterland of Split, and soon thereafter, a bit further to the south, towards Dubrovnik. Was that approximately your path in geographic terms?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then you occupied the position of Chief of Staff of the 4th Guards Brigade of the Croatian Army; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what exactly are staff affairs, staff work that you carried out?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: This is the work of planning, according to assignments given by the commander, work in supervision of the execution of the commander's decisions, work in providing professional and technical assistance in order to make sure that these missions and assignments are carried out as best possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As a rule what was the relationship between the Chief of Staff of a brigade and the commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff of a brigade is a professional assistant to the commander and the execution of his decisions. He can stand in for the commander in case of the latter's absence. And it is also the duty of a Chief of Staff to contribute to the implementation of the commander's idea by means of planning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say that he could stand in for the commander, does that mean that he could also be the deputy brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: If that unit did not have a deputy commander in reality or according to its establishment, then the Chief of Staff would carry out the duties of deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, is the deputy brigade commander inside the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No. If we look at the structure of the chain of command, the commander immediately supervises the commanders of the subordinate units, and the staff, as well as the deputy or his personal group, are lateral adjuncts, and they are not within that basic line of command, chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I believe that your reply did not enter the transcript exactly as you said. It says that the commanders of the subordinate unit are subordinate to the commander, and you mentioned also the staff and the deputy, et cetera. So it may be best if you would once again describe the chain of command as accurately as possible.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: In accordance with the principle of the unity of command, the commander, or the singleness of command, commands the commanders of subordinate units. And that's the chain of command. In that chain, there is neither a deputy nor a staff, but the commander commands them too. However, they do not command the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. It seems perfectly clear to me now. If the Judges have no questions, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A technical question. According to what you're saying, the Chief of Staff or the deputy to the commander have no authority over the chain of command. You say that it is the commander who has authority over the subordinate units. The Chief of Staff or the deputy to the commander are not in the chain of command stricto sensu, but let me give you a case study. Let's say that we have a commander, and unfortunately he has the flu and he's in ICU. He's totally unable, unfit to command. Who will take over the command over subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the commander is absent, the units are commanded by the deputy commander or the Chief of Staff in case there is no deputy commander. If -- or unless otherwise decided by somebody from the superordinate command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying that if the commander is absent, the deputy then takes over the command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, it may be good to define the notion of absence now so as to avoid any misunderstanding. Is the commander considered absent if he is not in his command but at some other place? What does "absent" mean?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Absent in this sense means that he is unable to command the units. When I said this, I didn't mean him not being present at the command post but, rather, being somewhere in the zone of operations or maybe in case he went to see his -- his high-ranking officer. These are not cases when his duties are shifted to either the deputy or the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let me take another example, another case study. Let's assume that the commander is abroad taking part in international negotiations. He is away from the territory. Could you tell us who is in command then on the territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be good practice in that case to empower the deputy and transfer the authority to command onto him in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And should there be a written order or is a verbal order sufficient, where the commander just tells his deputy, "I will be in Geneva in January and you will take over," or is there need for a very specific order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A written order is required, because that has to do, among other things, with the income to which the person is entitled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, if there is no written order, what can you say about the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, to my mind it follows only that the commander left suddenly and had no time to do what he should -- should have done. The deputy can be in a rather unpleasant situation if some drastic decisions have to be taken. Daily leadership and command, in order to implement decisions taken earlier, would be an area in which he could move without hindrance in exercising command duties, but going anywhere beyond that would be very risky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, this question of the chain of command is crucial, and I would like to get some detailed information on this. Does the commander convey his orders in a written form, as Judge Antonetti was asking, or can he also transmit orders verbally? And I'll put to you my second question also right away. If the orders can be conveyed orally, what happens to the -- to units like brigades or divisions? What about larger units? Isn't there a problem? The deputy commander and members of the staff maybe could also decide to give verbal orders and saying that these orders actually come from the commander but do not. And in the end, the soldiers executing these orders, are they able to check that these verbal orders were actually given by the commander heading the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly what I meant when I was saying that a written order should be in place about replacing -- or, rather, standing in for the commander. It isn't only about the authority of the commander. It also -- it's also about the implementation of the commander's order when he wants them executed -- orders when he wants them executed, because the deputy, too, while issuing written orders to his subordinates, in the letterhead of that order or that act will state: "Based on article so-and-so about general commanding, and the decision to stand in for the commander from, 'til, I issue the following order." Then, it will be clear to the subordinates that he is now exercising the function of commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about there is fraud, and by fraud head of staff or a member of the staff gives a verbal order to the units? Should the units actually carry out the order or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The units must carry out that order, and the commander of the unit, if he fosters doubts, can demand the verification of the authority of the deputy commander, especially if we're talking about orders that are not linked to the execution of previously defined tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. You perfectly answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us return to your biography, General. We are now approaching or coming closer to Bosnia. On the 4th of June, 1992, you became commander of the 116th Brigade of the Croatian Army, which was located at Metkovic. You first defend the transporter area of Eastern Herzegovina. You were defending the delta of the river Neretva from the east, and then you participated in the liberation of Stolac. In August 1992, you pull out of Stolac. You reorganise your brigade, and in September 1992, you take over command over the unit in the area of Popovo Polje in a narrow area along the Croatian border toward Dubrovnik. Is that an accurate summary, General?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes, but I must say that the unit that I commanded in the area of Zavala was still the 116th Brigade but downsized due to partial demobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We will speak that extensively in the continuation of this examination. Let us now continue with the biography. In March 1993, you leave the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and go to the command of the army district of Split; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please explain to us now the concept of army district. What was that territorial element of the Croatian Army called previously?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: It was called zone of operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it was zone of operations, and that's a synonym to army district; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, can you explain to us now what a zone of responsibility, and can the army district of Split -- can it be said of the army district of Split that the commander of that army district had a zone of responsibility there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Zone of operations is a notion from the operational layout of the battle-field. So that's a zone in which operations take place. And it -- when a commander gets his tasks, it is defined based on territorial points. The left and right limits are very precisely defined, and it includes an area both in the depth of enemy territory as well as in the depth of your own territory. You also asked me about the meaning of "army district."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I asked you, actually, about the area of responsibility. What would that term mean? Is the whole operation zone the area of responsibility of the commander of that operations zone or army district?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Before his answer, may I please interrupt. And first of all, good afternoon, Mr. President, and to each of Your Honours. We have been dealing with this evidence now of this witness for an hour. The only matter that features on the two summaries that have been provided to the Prosecution is the fact that's not in dispute, that this gentleman took place in the liberation of Stolac in 1992. We've dealt with All People's Defence, with Zadar and Milivoj Petkovic's role there, with the League of Communists in the JNA, with the work of the Chief of Staff of the brigade and the chain of command, and now we're moving on to deal with army districts, and I have sat, I hope, reasonably patiently because they seem, with respect, to me to be matters that were either peripheral or matters which the Prosecution didn't need notice of, but I must raise at this stage the fact that having asked for an additional summary in respect of this witness and having been given one, we've been given none of this whatsoever, and I'm afraid on behalf of the Prosecution I have to object to us pursuing any more lines that are going to take up -- lines of examination that are going to take us into detailed, and if they are important, then important issues in the case without the Prosecution having the least chance to prepare itself for them. And I would invite the Court to direct Ms. Alaburic to return to the topics that are summarised in the two summaries which we have been provided with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave I would like to respond to my learned friend. I believe that it is one of the elementary rules that if the witness tells us he was Chief of Staff of a brigade, to ask him what exactly that means, what kind of work he performed, and what his position in the chain of command was. The witness's answers, if they are judged as good by the Trial Chamber, will be important for us when viewing any future Chief of Staff we meet and his place in the chain of command. If Mr. Beneta tells us that he had worked in an officers' training centre, he should be allowed to tell us about his work in the training centre as a part of the concept of All People's Defence. This is no surprise, and we intend to discuss it with every future Defence witness because this is extremely relevant to our Defence case. What Mr. Beneta is telling us now is an explanation of the whole set of categories that we have dealt before in this courtroom, and what we want to do now is get a precise definition of terms. The topic of the area of responsibility has been discussed at great length by every participant in this courtroom, and now we have before us a highly qualified general who is in a good position to explain to us what that means in the Croatian Army and in NATO standards, what an area of responsibility is or isn't. This is the last generally military -- general military question I intend to ask and then we'll move on to the Croatian Army and Croatian troops. But before I move on to that, I would like Mr. Beneta to explain to us what exactly an area of responsibility is and what its significance is in the execution of military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: May I reply just very briefly to that and say that nobody disputes that -- that this general is well placed to say things which might be important. That's not my objection. My objection is simply this: If they are important, then they should have been provided to the Prosecution in advance as the rules and this Chamber's guidance clearly state.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I informed my learned friends from the Prosecution and all Defence teams of all the facts that this witness will be speaking to. What we are dealing with now are definitions of categories, because at one point when the witness tells us where he was in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the 116th Brigade, we will be discussing with him his area of responsibility. Therefore, I thought it was a good idea to clarify the term now in the introductory part. We can clarify it, of course later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I will not discuss whether it was a good idea or not, but you have indicated what the witness was going to testify about. This question of zone of operation and area, we have extensively spoken with another military expert who has just testified the last two weeks, and I think that the objection is justified and should be upheld. So please proceed to address the questions that you have actually said that you would address.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Beneta, then tell us then, please, when with the 116th Brigade you took up positions at Popovo Polje on the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, what was your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: My area of responsibility was a section of the front line limited on the left and on the right side. Behind my own lines it was the area where I deployed my forces, and behind enemy lines it reached up to the possible limit of my action.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. You will show us later on the map, and that will be the end of it. Let me now finish with your curriculum vitae. In the summer of 1993, for about a month, you were engaged in one military operation of the Croatian Defence Council in Bosnia and Herzegovina, after which you returned to the army district of Split where you took up position of commander of Operations Group Sibenik for 22 months; Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the last point: You were chief of anti-aircraft defence in the Croatian navy and deputy chief of the operations zone of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army for modernisation. Then you were commander of the centre for international military operations. After that, commander of the school of warfare. And as you said in response to a question by Judge Antonetti, you are now deputy chief inspector in the defence inspectorate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll now move to the next subject with a working title as follows: "Departure of Croatian soldiers to Bosnia and Herzegovina During Wartime." Do you have your set of documents in front of you, General? Look at 3D343. Have you found it, General? This is a letter signed by Petar Stipetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not the right document in the electronic courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you mean 443?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Correct. I misspoke. It's 443. My mistake. 3D443, a letter by General Petar Stipetic, dated 8th of April, 1992. I'll ask you very specific questions. Based on this document, to whom was it sent?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: It was sent to the Operation Zone Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At that time were you in that operation zone?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I was chief of the -- Chief of Staff of the 4th Guards Brigade in that operation zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us the beginning of this letter that says: "Subject: Your act." What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: That means that somebody from the operations zone, let's say a commander of the operations zone, had sent some sort of dispatch to the Main Staff, and here in this letter - which is a response - they cite the reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From the contents of this document which approves the departure of volunteers from the Croatian Army to Bosnia and Herzegovina, what could you conclude about the contents of the original query sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Well, that query was a summary of requests from units, and one of those units was my brigade, the 4th Brigade, namely that a position be taken urgently on the situation prevailing in the units at the time. Namely, a certain number of soldiers in my unit, and I believe it was the same in most other units, were young men who were living in Croatia or in Herzegovina, both natives of Herzegovina who had joined the fight against the Serbian aggressor and the Yugoslav People's Army and who reacted in the circumstances that had obviously changed in the areas where their parents lived and exercised enormous pressure to be allowed to go to fight in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What would have happened if these young men, these soldiers, had not been allowed to go fight in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: I think they would have gone anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If all your soldiers hailing from Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time, in the beginning of April 1994, in your unit and in other units, if all of them had gone to fight in Bosnia and Herzegovina of their own accord, what would have happened with the units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: First of all, our strength would have been significantly diminished without any prospect of replenishment in the near future.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, can we specify the period? Is it April 1999 -- 1992? We seem to have an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you now explain if the units of the Croatian Army were in such danger, if all the natives of Bosnia and Herzegovina left, did you have any interest in -- in organising this in a different way?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. It was in our interest to do it in organised fashion for a number of reasons. Shall I explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: At that point we had been carrying out military operations for eight months already. We had built something that was very difficult to build, and that was a tight knit military group that had grown in the war. To let those men leave in a haphazard way would have meant that each of them would have gone to their birthplace and tried of their own accord to organise some sort of resistance or save their parents, something like that. If they had gone like that, just by deserting, going AWOL, we would have had a problem with resolving their status later. We would have trouble admitting them back into the unit a month later if -- just as if nothing had happened. And in addition, those of them who had families in Croatia, wives, children, would have been deprived of income.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, General. Let us look at P153 now. P153. That's also a letter by General Stipetic. To whom was this one sent?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The letter was sent to the commander of the zone of operations of Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph mention is made of both Croats and Muslims who want to go and defend Bosnia and Herzegovina as volunteers. Tell us, General, from your own experience, too, did you treat Croatian soldiers of Croatian ethnicity and of Muslim ethnicity the same way or did you distinguish between them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: In my unit I had about 20 to 30 per cent of Croats hailing from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I also had Muslims who were residents of Croatia or who were from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there was no difference with regard to our position about letting them go.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document about this topic. It's 3D299. It's a document by Colonel Hasan Efendic from an office of Bosnia-Herzegovina, sent to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. It is requested that three officers of the Croatian Army, mentioned by name here, be allowed to go, although it is risky to judge about a person's ethnicity based on their name, but what would you say about the ethnicity of these persons mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: All these three persons are almost certainly of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph it says: "We are asking you to resolve the status of these officers, as has been the case so far, by putting their status on hold, and after fulfilling their tasks, they should be allowed to continue serving in the Croatian Army." General, if you were asked to interpret what this "as has been the case so far" means with regards to the practice of letting officers of Muslim ethnicity go to BiH --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Taking into consideration the date, the Croatian Army had for several months permitted people to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina individually because they were obviously needed there and this document obviously refers to that practice, and it is requested that three more persons be permitted to go in accordance with the same principle. That is to keep their status in the Croatian Army, and after fulfilling their task, they should have the opportunity to continue their career in the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So we can conclude, General, at this time in 1992, did you have any knowledge or did you observe any instances of discrimination of officers of Muslim ethnicity in the Republic of Croatia who wanted to join the Territorial Defence or subsequently the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I had an assistant. That is, he was the chief of pioneers in the brigade, who, after eight months that he had spent in my unit, requested to be permitted to go to Sarajevo. He was let go. He never even asked for his status to be put on hold. He -- he went to -- with no regard to that, and there were no problems for him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, General, the let us pass on to the next topic the working title of which is "The Croatian Army on the Territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One in a moment, General. I'd like to still look at this document which is dated the 4th of January, 1993. The date is important. It is signed by Colonel Hasan Efendic. If I'm not mistaken, Colonel Hasan Efendic was commander of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina before being replaced by Halilovic. Is that the same person as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know anything about the succession of their duties. I never followed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know. This document states that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had an office in Zagreb. We have the address of this office, Savska Cesta, number 41. We have a phone number also. This document states that there is a request for help submitted to the Ministry of Defence, Croatian Ministry of Defence, for the latter to second three people who will keep the same status within the Croatian Army. As far as you know, at the end of 1993, in the early months of 1993, the Croatian Army, did it actually provide at the request of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina soldiers and officers, or, as far as you know, was it the case that at the end of 1992, in the early months of 1993 -- there is mistake on the transcript, I said end of 1992 and in the early months of 1993, did the Croatian Army actually send soldiers and officers to reinforce the HVO against the ABiH and only in those cases? How did things stand as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I was busy in the 4th Brigade, and later on I also was engaged with the 116th Brigade in Eastern Herzegovina. So I was on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina with my unit. My estimate is that we went as deep as 20 or 25 kilometres [realtime transcript read in error "metres"] into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I continue. You probably want to know about the situation not there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand how there can be mistakes on the transcript like that. You said 20 to 25 kilometres and it states "20 to 25 metres" on the transcript. You have to be very careful. Everything a witness says is important. Is it 20 to 25 kilometres or is it 20 to 25 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 20 to 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to be extremely careful. Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that your question is not focused on that but whether or not there were members of the Croatian Army who were let go and who were going deeper into the territory individually or in an organised fashion, regardless of holding on the defence line toward Croatia in the territory along the border. Yes, I know that there were departures as a consequence of pressure exerted for the people to be let go, because we were faced with arguments -- with such arguments that left me no choice than to let those people go. If I made a mistake or not, I don't know. I thought that was -- this way I would contribute to the resolution of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interrupting you because you are developing a number of points, but there are salient features which are important. When you are 20 to 25 metres [as interpreted] in depths, what dates are you talking about? 20 to 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the period from the first half of 1992 'til -- well, almost until the end of the war speaking about the southern front, but that that depth was reduced to 2 to 4 kilometres at certain spots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're saying until the end of the war, but give us a date, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the end of 1995, September, October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're telling us, and you're under oath, that your unit was in depth in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and still under oath you are telling us that you were 20 to 25 kilometres in depth and this was reduced to some 4 kilometres. Now, here's my question: When you received the order to go over there, to go in another country, in a country which is not the Republic of Croatia, what were you told exactly, "You are going there to face the Serbs," or "You're going there to attack the Muslims"? Could you tell us exactly what was the content of the military order which you received allowing you to go in depth in a foreign country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order was to defend the territory of Croatia and a constituent part of the order were also geographical maps. It was clear from that that we were to take positions from which we can successfully defend a relatively narrow stretch of territory between the state border and the coastline and which would at the same time allow us enough manoeuvre space.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, everything the witness has said now we put on a map which we will show to you, and we will show you documents. We will also try to explain the reasons and the legitimacy of this way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is time for the break. We will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court is back in session. General, before giving the floor to Ms. Alaburic, I have a follow-up question. You're telling us that you were 20 to 25 kilometres in depth. Could you tell us whether there were civilians in that territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were also civilians in that territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There were civilians, but these were not Croatian citizens. These were civilians who lived in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, maybe you know this or you don't, and if you do, all the better because it will be easier, and if you don't, well, I'll tell you about it. We have a regulation, a 1907, The Hague regulation, and Article 42 of this regulation says, and I will quote it slowly: "A territory is considered as occupied when it is placed de facto under the authority of the enemy army. The occupation is only -- is only for the place where the authority is located and where the authority can be exercised." So when you were occupying this 20 to 25 kilometres in depth, did you feel like you were exercising an authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In part. As unit commander I came across situations when I had to deal with certain issues that could be qualified as issues of authority seeking to hand it over to the civilian authorities as soon as possible if the system had been disrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me continue with my question. There is another article in the 1907 regulation, Article 43: "The authority of the legal -- of legal power being now in the hands of the occupying power, the latter will take all measures depending from it in order to re-establish and to ensure, as far as possible, law and order while abiding, unless possible, the rules in place in the country." When you were in depth in that territory did you take any measures to re-establish law and order and public life in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me finish off. As you know, officers of the German Army were tried by American courts, and there is a very famous judgement, appeals judgement, US v. Pohl and it says the following, and I'll quote it and you'll understood: "The rules of war impose on all military officers who are in command the positive obligation to take all possible measures suitable to the circumstances in order to control those who are under his command and to prevent all actions that may lead to infringements of the rules of war." When you were in a foreign territory, when you were stationed in depth in this foreign territory, did you take any measures against your own soldiers to make sure that these would not commit any infringement of -- any acts that would be against the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In all foreseeable situations, I did take such measures, and I never had any need to take subsequent measures because there were no cases of disciplinary infractions in such a form that anyone would be hurt, especially not civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your answer is very specific. I will finish off with one simple question. When you were occupying this territory, this 20 to 25 territory in depth, were there any combats in that zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm putting this question to you about the combat, because when Belgium was occupied by Germany, the areas of responsibility were broken in three, areas where combats were under way. There the authority was the military authority a hundred per cent. And then there was another area, the reserve area, where authority was jointly exercised between the civilians and the military. And there was a third zone, the rest of Belgium, where the only authority was the civilian authority. The occupying power, of course, but civilian occupying power managing this area, which is why I'm asking you whether there were any combats in your own zone, and you said there were. So in this zone, this area where combats were occurring, did you believe that you were the only person liable or responsible and that no civilian authority was in charge of anything in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My operations and combat activity that I pursued there was conducted in co-operation with the populous in that area, and I did not have all the elements of an occupying power, nor did I have to exercise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can tell you that you have now touched upon absolutely all the subjects that I wanted to cover in my examination. I would just kindly ask the Trial Chamber to trust us to examine our witnesses both on the Hague Conventions and the principles of occupation, and that we will honestly and openly demonstrate all the circumstances we believe relevant. And before I resume my examination, I would only like to intervene on the transcript. The question of Judge Antonetti on page 29 related to the fact that Croatia was sending officers and troops into Bosnia and Herzegovina. The witness started to answer in line 12, 13, and 14 on page 29, and a part of his answer was not recorded; namely, that Croatia approved the departure of these soldiers and officers to Bosnia and Herzegovina. We will correct the transcript later, but it is now important to make this straight for the sake of everyone's understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We will now, using documents and maps, try to demonstrate all that all you, Witness, have told us so far. Last week, Witness, we had a Defence expert for Generals Praljak and Petkovic Defence, and in document 4D1731 he explained that under certain circumstances a state has the right to enter the territory of another state if it had been attacked from the territory of that other state. Following up on that position, I will ask you a very specific question. Let us assume that the Republic of Croatia is targeted from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, let's say from the environs of Trebinje. Let us define that it is the Army of Republika Srpska attacking the Republic of Croatia. Now, tell us, in the normal course of things what would the Republic of Croatia be expected to do to stop these attacks from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: It would be necessary to do exactly what I eventually received as a military assignment, namely to nip the threat in the bud, that is, to enter the territory from which we are targeted up to a point from which it is possible to make sure that these attacks would be terminated. Remove the sources of threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, under international law, at least as described in the manuals of the Yugoslav People's Army, what is considered to be a theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: A theatre of war is the entire territory covered by the warring parties in that war. Namely, the territories of states are A and B if these states are at war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So if the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina up to Trebinje, from which Croatia is targeted, is defined by the term "theatre of war," would it be correct to say that the territory of Croatia, which is targeted, like the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina from which the attacks originate, is considered as one theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. Both these territories of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina are theatres of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Look now at the next document, 4D1483. It's a map showing plans of the Yugoslav People's Army from May 1991, and it was made by our military expert, Milan Gorjanc, and from this map we can see that it was planned from north via Livno to move towards Split, and in the area of Split, cut through the territory of the republic -- of the Republic of Croatia and completely isolate the territory south of Split. And it was also planned from the south side, from the direction of Stolac and this part of Herzegovina, to move towards the sea and then link up these forces of the JNA from the south and the north and completely isolate Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Republic of Croatia. Now, my question, General Beneta, is this: Did you have information that the Yugoslav People's Army in mid-1991 had such plans of combat activity relating to this part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. I had that information, because one of my assistants, now General Mirko Sundov, was working -- had worked in the Territorial Defence before the war broke out, and he told me about this plan called S2 that had been developed as a sort of contingency plan in case Yugoslavia was attacked from that side. However, it is clear from everything that it was in fact a military plan to enter the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we go back to April 1992 when many soldiers, members of the HV who hailed from BiH want to go to defend their homeland, BiH, was there a military activity from the army -- by the Army of the Republika Srpska much along the same lines as these that we see on the northern end of this map? Namely, from the direction of Kupres and Livno?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: I personally didn't take part in activities regarding the area up there, but I knew that the JNA did manoeuvre in order to mass troops around Kupres, and they wanted to bring as many troops there as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will show you a map now, 4D1351 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have the map in front of me like everyone else. Ms. Alaburic told us that this map was -- was a plan, intervention plan, May 1991, and she asked you whether in April 1992 the Republika Srpska had the same plan, and you answered by saying that you didn't know, but I thought I understood that it would have been normal for Republika Srpska to do exactly the same thing from Kupres to Livno. Now, when looking at this map, I was listening to what you said earlier regarding this single battle-field, saying Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were one battle-field. Does this mean that for the Republic of Croatia to be able to defend itself it had militarily, and I insist on the word "militarily," to penetrate into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in depth in this territory, otherwise it would find itself in dire straits and could maybe be squeezed out of the territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to point out to the Chamber that part of this plan had already been carried out through the attacks of the JNA. The southern-most arrow pointing towards Slano had been implemented in October 1991, and only after that did the Croatian forces that were only being created had grown barely strong enough to bar the enemy from go -- from going any further. So it was the task of the unit of which I was commander, or Chief of Staff, to do the following: After the south of Croatia had been occupied and Dubrovnik cut off, we were in a situation where the south of Croatia was occupied except for the town of Dubrovnik itself. That was fighting off attacks in the outskirts of town. With regard to the northern part, the area of Kupres, there was an entire corps, and it was especially conspicuous to see the movement of an armour brigade toward Kupres, which didn't have any barracks up there or any other accommodation, but it was ad hoc, being moved there in order to create favourable conditions for the implementation of this plan thought out by the JNA before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, as a final question, I was listening to you and I would like to know the following: If the Serbian forces had reached Split, can we infer from this that militarily the Republic of Croatia would have been in jeopardy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would have meant the occupation of some 15 to 20 per cent of the territory of Croatia, only in this part. A similar situation was in existence in Western Slavonia or in the area of Vukovar. All that put into jeopardy the crucial interest of the Republic of Croatia, namely integrity and sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, what was the only way for Croatia to try and liberate this occupied southern part around Dubrovnik and further south and protect itself from possible aggression on the territory around Split and southward? So what was the way to -- for Croatia to protect itself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The only possible way was military intervention. And I must stress that in the area from Ston and Slano southward, that military intervention is next to impossible if it takes place only in the area between the coastline and the state border.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, how broad is that territory?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Down there the territory has an average width of 5 kilometres, ranging from 15 kilometres down to only 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, is this a mountainous area or is it a plain?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The area is mountainous, and there is only one road communication, which is entirely on Croatian territory. There is also an unpaved road which is higher in the mountains, but it runs partly through Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Croatia -- for Croatia there was no other way to defend itself but send troops to the territory of BiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the next map, 4D1351. Take a look at the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could give the witness a pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, this is a map showing the deployment of HVO forces. Furthermore, forces of the HV as opposed to the VRS and the JNA. The date is the 30th of April, 1992. We have already seen this map in the proofing so that you're familiar with it. Tell us whether this map reflects the deployment of the units of the HV on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Could you repeat the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes, it does reflect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark on this map where exactly your command post was. If I'm not mistaken, you were still in the 4th Guard Brigade.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. The command of the brigade was here at Hutovo. I'm marking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please put a number 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So number 1, Hutovo where the command of the 4th Guard Brigade was, commanded by the witness. Could we please have an IC number for this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The marked version of document 4D1351 shall be given Exhibit IC1096. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I now ask the usher to bring this map to the witness and put it on the ELMO. Your Honours, we made this map for you. The witness saw it during the proofing and he will explain it to you, and we'll use it in order to reduce the time necessary to discuss these issues. It's the same map that we saw a minute ago, and now we'll see which combat activity and what kind of combat activity took place there by mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, there are territories here marked A, B, and C.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that there are problems with the ELMO. All right. Maybe we can move on. If it can be fixed, then we'll go back to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Since the Trial Chamber has this map and perhaps the ELMO can be repaired in the meantime, General, tell us what you wanted to show on this map. What do the letters A, B, and C mark?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The letter A, the southern letter A, that is, marks the territory which was liberated by the 4th and the 1st Brigades of the Croatian Army in the end of May and in early June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Ms. Alaburic, we do not have the map. We cannot see it, I think, so it's very difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we'll skip that, Your Honours, and meanwhile we'll fix the ELMO. But I want to say that this map shows the activities involved in the liberation of the southern part of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina in one part, and the liberation of Dubravska Visoravan in one part, and the Stolac operation in which the witness took part. That's the territory that's 25 kilometres deep. I hope the ELMO can be fixed so that we can speak about it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, the last operation that we'll show on this map is the liberation of Stolac. When you spoke about an area that is 20 to 25 kilometres deep in which forces of the HV were engaged, did you mean those operations, that is the liberation of the Dubravska Visoravan and Stolac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you carry out these operations in co-operation with the Territorial Defence or the ABiH, respectively; that is, with the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the following document: P339. It's an agreement about friendship and co-operation signed by Alija Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman of the 21st of July, 1992. Tell us, General, this date July the 21st, was this after all these liberation operations that we mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let us go back to the map which we now have on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we could move it up so we can see all of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, the area you marked A.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: This area here and this area were liberated in the same operation when the forces of the HV started moving toward Dubrovnik -- Dubrovnik. It was from the 28th or 29th of May 'til the 4th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the territory marked B?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: This territory was liberated round about the 6th of June, 1992. Maybe a day earlier or later. That is immediately after the completion of the operations in which the A territories were liberated. Here, too, the forces of the HV and those of the HVO acted jointly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the Muslim population co-operate with you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: In the area marked A there weren't really any Muslims. And about area B, I have no direct knowledge because I didn't take part in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the territory marked C?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: For this territory I led the combat operations, and a battalion composed of people who live at Stolac and the surrounding areas marked B were the ones who were involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: They were mostly Croats, because they were driven out when the Serbian forces moved into territory B, Domanovici, and the people expelled established a unit of the strength of a battalion. They -- it was organised by their local authorities. They went through training, and they took part in the liberation of their towns and villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was that battalion joined by the population of Stolac of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The operation was carried out in such a manner that 200 men in the night of the 11th of June, 1992, were allowed to enter Stolac by the assistance of the Muslim population that remained to live in Stolac, which was under Serbian occupation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll go into the details later. For the time being, it matters to me that these were joint actions carried out by Croats and Muslims. And the territory marked C was also liberated in June 1992. Is that so, General?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It was from the 13th to the 15th of June thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, please put today's date on the map, sign it, and perhaps we can get an IC number.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The second map marked portion of the map shall be given Exhibit IC1097. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we now please come back to this document P339, the agreement on friendship and co-operation, of 21st July, 1992, signed by Izetbegovic and Tudjman. So it was signed about a month after all these actions of liberation. Let us look together at item 8, please. In item 8 it is noted that the aggression of the Serbian and Montenegrin military forces against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is continuing, but also largely against the Republic of Croatia from the contiguous areas of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My question, General, the authorities under Izetbegovic at that time, did they have the power to intervene at the time in the areas from which Croatia was attacked?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No. The estimate at the time, and even when you analyse it now, everything indicates that they did not have the ability to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At that time had there ever been any objections to the joint military actions by the Croatian Army, the HVO, and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was still called the Territorial Defence at the time in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No. There had been no objection to these interventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about Alija Izetbegovic, the Muslim populous of those areas and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did they ever consider the Croatian Army an aggressor?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. I can only recall the excellent co-operation both on the part of the Muslim population and the authority of both ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 4D1240 is our next document. It's a directive from the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, signed by Sefer Halilovic. What we want to know at this time is item III where neighbours are defined, and those are the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia. And then it says that: "These armed forces, by executing offensive operations to liberate the territory of parts of Croatia with the part of their forces engaged in the area of Dubrovnik, coordinate most immediately with our forces in the liberation of Eastern Herzegovina, especially the towns of Trebinje and Stolac." General, can you comment on this position of the man number one in the Supreme Command Staff of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: This is essentially correct, although I would put it even more accurately perhaps. In this paragraph the focus is a bit different. From this paragraph you would understand that the main vehicle of this action is the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whereas in fact you could say that the Croatian Army had done more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But there is no dispute that this was a joint action of the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No dispute whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, 4D1353.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I noticed a paragraph which could be of interest on page 4. Roman numeral III. There it is. It says that: "The armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, conducting offensive operations to liberate Croatian territory ..." General, this document, stems from the supreme commander of the armed forces in Sarajevo, seems to admit that the Republic of Croatia is conducting a military operation to liberate its territory. This is what it says in writing, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's precisely what we read there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
