utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then it says that -- Trebinje and Stolac are mentioned, as well as the area of Dubrovnik, Dubrovnik sector. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, if we wanted to define all these localities mentioned also by Judge Antonetti from the point of view of theatre of war, it's not only a unified single theatre of war but a single battle zone.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. This was declared as the southern theatre of war by the Croatian command, and it includes both parties in these -- in this territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look now at the next document, 4D1353. It's a map developed on the basis of this document by Sefer Halilovic we have just looked at. It was made by General Petkovic. Could you now on this map, which is also on the screen, mark where at that time, and that was September 1992, your unit was, that is, the Croatian Army was.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: September 1992, the Croatian Army was in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you put letters HV there and sign.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would ask for an IC number for this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have an IC number for the map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The marked version of document 4D1353 shall be given Exhibit IC1098. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, we'll look at two documents, skipping the next one, to see what was going on with you in your unit. First P326. It's an order issued on the 13th July, 1992, signed by Janko Bobetko, sent also to TG-2. It says "Colonel Beneta." Tell me, what orders did you receive herein?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: This order orders me to hand over the defence positions around the town of Stolac to the Croatian Defence Council. In fact, also the unit that was then in defence positions were to be handed over to the 1st Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify in follow-up to the question by Judge Antonetti. In legal terms you were entering Stolac as an occupying force, and you had certain special powers as a military commander. What happened with these special powers after the hand-over of Stolac? Did you continue to hold these powers or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No, I no longer had any of those powers. I had turned over both the area of responsibility and the forces defending that area to the 1st Brigade of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next document, 4D1406. It's an order from Milivoj Petkovic, dated 1st August 1992, and item 1 says that by 7 August 1992, the sectors of defence of the 116th and the 114th Brigades of the Croatian Army shall be taken over by units from Grude, Ljubuski, and Citluk. What happened following this order?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: I am aware of it, and pursuant to that order I turned over also that area that a unit of the Croatian Army under me was holding north of Stolac, marked on the map as north A. That part, too, I handed over to a unit of the HVO, and I moved lower to defend Slano, taking up positions to the left and right of a place called Zavala, towards the exit in the direction of Popovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This place Slano is in the territory of which state?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: It's a coastal settlement in the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask the usher to show the witness another map to be placed on the ELMO. I hope it will work this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, you're telling us that you handed over to the HVO all your powers. The document is fairly clear on that. The area you were occupying, is this a part of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Well, it is. So why did you not hand over your authority to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Why did you hand your authority over to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time in that area there was no BH Army, none. There were only forces of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let's assume that if the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been there, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I tell you before that a situation that actually happened, and then I'll answer your question? When I was planning the operation to liberate Stolac, I had assistance from Muslims who had remained in Stolac under Serb occupation. When we were mounting and preparing our defence, the Muslims joined the Croatian Defence Council and defended their hometown. At one point a man called Mahmutcehajic wanted to form a unit of the BH Army in Stolac. I enabled him to do so, and I asked that proportionally to the strength of the unit he was forming he take over a part of the front line, because I thought it was fair. Three or four days later, around 30 young men, mainly Muslims, came to the command of the sector that I had formed and asked to be included in a that unit that I had positioned in defence, saying that they were not going to set up any army just because an individual wanted it to be so, and they had no equipment, no uniforms. And after that I went back to that man and asked him if he still wanted to stick with his original plan or he wanted to join the joint defence. He agreed, and he became assistant commander of the Stolac sector for logistics. No one would have been happier than I had we been able, had we had the wherewithal to create a unit of the BH Army that would have taken up part of the front line, because my men were getting killed every day defending that line. That attempt failed not because of my unwillingness, but because of the local people who wanted instead to join a force that in that area was the best prepared, the best trained, the best equipped, the most experienced.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now we can deal with the map on the ELMO. Tell me, did you draw this map over the past few days when we were preparing for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what this map shows?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: This map shows the situation from September 1992 onwards. Conditionally, I divided it into two parts. I'm showing the first part now where one unit of the Croatian Army was still holding positions. Very shortly afterwards, within a month, that unit, too, turned over that area of responsibility to an HVO unit. I think it was the Ravno Battalion. And this Croatian Army unit withdrew to the shaded area I'm showing now. I shaded only the area on the other side of the border that belongs to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and somewhere in that area that's how the border went, and important topographic features were taken on both sides of the border and defence was held throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina is this black line; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what is the width of this territory at the beginning of this section that is strongly shaded?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: When you climb up the macadam road, up the hill, for one kilometre approximately, that's where the border is. And then it varies from 4 kilometres to 8 kilometres all the way up to Dubrovnik. Sorry, 4 kilometres to 800 metres all the way to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, can you repeat when you were talking about the width -- it's now been -- it's now been corrected. Thank you. This territory that you're talking about, it's between the sea and the Bosnian border.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the territory between the sea and the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the positions of Croatian forces were either a bit further south inside Croatian territory or a bit more forward up to 1, 1.5 kilometres. It depended more on topography than on the physical border itself, because soldiers simply have their own rules of action and they cannot take up positions in a depression just because the border lies there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us define for the Judges, General, the width of this area inside Bosnian territory at the narrowest point and at the widest point.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The widest point would be precisely from Slano towards Zavala, around 8 kilometres, and the narrow part would be 100 metres from the border. The front line was inside the Croatian territory, actually, which we can't see on the map because topography did not allow it any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sign this map, too, General, and then I would like to ask for a number.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a technical question. I don't have the Strugar indictment at hand when he bombed Dubrovnik. However, could you tell us whether what you have mentioned occurred before or after the bombing of Dubrovnik? Did you understand my question? We have a map here on the ELMO where we see Dubrovnik and the front line. I would like to know whether this map was drawn before or after the shelling of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the shelling of Dubrovnik lasted for quite a while, so I can't tell you that this happened on a certain date. This was the situation after Croatian forces lifted the blockade of Dubrovnik. Thus from the area of Slano -- or, rather, Ston, a breakthrough was made towards Dubrovnik, and a bit later the conditions were created for a noncombat takeover in the south with a minor skirmish only, and this situation here is following all that, after the Croatian forces successfully controlled not only the ground forces of infantry but also tried to control the enemy artillery to stop them from shelling Dubrovnik, because they were still doing it occasionally with the largest calibres. However, we did not take any offensive operations because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You answered my question. Now I would like to know the following: If the Croatian Army had not been positioned as it is here on the map, above Dubrovnik, then the service -- the Serbian forces would have been close to Dubrovnik and it would have placed Dubrovnik in jeopardy, and you said that was the reason why they used heavy artillery to shell Dubrovnik. Was that the gist of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They shelled Dubrovnik with heavy artillery before this area was liberated. There was even direct shooting from smaller calibres. They reduced their activity to the greater calibres only when we pushed them away from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I understand you correctly, this is the first time that I'm looking into the situation of Dubrovnik. If I understand correctly, if the Croatian Army hadn't been there, Dubrovnik would have been in jeopardy because the Serbian forces would have invaded the territory of BiH where the BiH -- where the ABiH was not present, and could have easily shelled and attacked Dubrovnik, which is why the Croatian Army had to be present in this area. Is this what you're trying to convey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is the very essence the military situation. Not because I say so, but it was like that on the ground. Dubrovnik was literally hanging on a thread. The only connection that we had with Dubrovnik, which was a pearl of Croatian culture, was by sea and at night, and we used small and fast vessels to -- to go through the Yugoslav navy vessels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Alaburic, but I would I like to have a follow-up question only. Here what we are having in front of us as far as the map is concerned, it is from August 1992. My question is that - I'm not very familiar now as far as the dates are concerned with Dubrovnik - if when the siege of Dubrovnik has been terminated by the Croatian army, it is what I would like to ask you, was it before 1992 August or afterwards, if you remember the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The attack operation on the southern theatre of war to liberate Dubrovnik started on the 30th or 31st of May, 1992. It lasted three to four days, and we broke through enemy positions on both sides of the border, that is from the coastline all the way to Popovo Polje, and hereabouts the forces were stopped partly due to the intervention of the international community, I believe. And after a few months, but I can't give you an exact date, after long and tough negotiations an agreement was signed on a ship of the international forces, I don't know which country it belonged to. So there was an agreement between General Bobetko and the enemy force, that they would leave the entire area all the way to Prevlaka, but the agreement didn't define all -- any elements, because it mentioned a -- the departure of the Yugoslav People's Army, but the plan was for the forces from the Republika Srpska, that is from a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to enter that area suddenly, which would have meant that the agreement had been honoured, technically, but Croatia wouldn't have gotten back its territory. When the agreement entered into force, the Croatian forces landed from the sea in that area and soon reached a topographically significant area. There was a brief fighting and we were able to -- to take the Serbian forces by surprise and put the territory -- territory under our control where it remained until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need an IC number for this map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The map just marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC1099. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, just for the sake of a better understanding of the map, let us explain once more. Once we draw a borderline, we assume that everybody knows where the border is, so please confirm that the black line that you drew is the international border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Perhaps we should return the map. My friend Mr. Stewart has just told me that it all just isn't clear enough. So if I could ask the usher to oblige. Could we put the map back on the ELMO, please, and I'll also ask my friend Mr. Stewart to keep an eye on everything to see whether everything is clear. General, let's proceed in the following manner: Mark the territory of the Republic of Croatia with a number 1.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can use a marker that is more conspicuous.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So a number 1 to mark the territory of Croatia. And now please write BiH on the territory that belongs to that country.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. And now please show us which is territory controlled by Serbian authorities including the VRS.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The red line is the one representing it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: East of this dotted red line is the territory controlled by the forces of the Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, please put a number 2 on the territory controlled by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now let's go to the part of Bosnia and Herzegovina controlled by the Muslim and Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The Muslim and Croatian authorities control this part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I will mark it with a number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. When I look at the map, did you not put the H of Herzegovina into Serb-controlled area? The H of BiH, it is not on a territory now which is actually controlled by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we wanted to say that this is the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the country, irrespective of the effective control, and the number 2 stands for the Serbs, and the number 3 for Croats and Muslims. I believe that it is clear now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right. And now there is another document about this subject, and I believe we'll be able to deal with it until the break. So the document number is 4D475. We have already seen the document in this -- in this courtroom. It is a document by Miljenko Lasic, the commander of the zone of operations of South-east Herzegovina and under item 3, which is on page 3 for you, he describes his neighbours. It reads: "To the south, right-hand side of us, defence is organised by the 116th Brigade of the Croatian Army." Tell us, General, is this position of your brigade as stated here, does it coincide with what we have just seen on that map?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. This is that situation briefly described, but don't be confused by this -- by this language "south" and in brackets, "right-hand side," because it was actually to the south-east.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And if we recall your biography, then we'll see that you stayed there until March 1993 on these positions, namely, and then you returned to Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, did the brigade -- or the Croatian Army stay there until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And there wasn't significant movement, and I've already explained how the Croatian Army forces entered the southern areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to go into the liberation of Stolac now, so this may be a convenient moment for a break and then start a new subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. It's time for a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Stewart, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly. Your Honour, the Prosecution have put in a list. There's only one item on it for an exhibit to be tendered through -- to be admitted that was tendered through Witness Gorjanc, the expert witness. We have put in our IC list in the normal way asking for a number of items. Each of these submissions requires a little bit more than the usual thought and response, and I've discussed it with Mr. Stringer. Your Honour, subject to Your Honours' approval, we would ask that we each have until Thursday to respond to give our objections to the other's application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber is extending the deadline to Thursday. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let us now go into the issue of the liberation of Stolac. Although, you have already said something about that, but we'll try to deal with it systematically. Tell us, to start with, the OTP in these proceedings has tried to put forward several times the thesis that there was no fighting for Stolac, that the Serbs merely walked out of Stolac, and that it may be the outcome of some kind of agreement between the Serbs and the Croats. Can you, as an eyewitness, say what -- what this was all about? Was there any fighting at Stolac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: There was fighting for Stolac in which three of my soldiers were killed, and there were several dozen wounded. The commander of the defence of Stolac, a major by rank, in the VRS was killed and one of his staff officers, and three other staff members of his were taken prisoner. There was fighting for each and every position around Stolac, and I must admit that I am astonished by such a view. We began the operation in such a way that the intelligence organ of the 116th Brigade agreed with the Muslim population from Stolac to accommodate a number of my fighters and hide them away until the beginning of the attack. I didn't expect it, but it happened that the Muslim representatives of the authority, anticipating an attack, sent over -- sent a significant number of civilians to my side of the confrontation line, and so we asked the -- our high command to organise and provide buses, and this population that had fled Stolac was moved out of my area of responsibility and out of the range of artillery. After that, the attack started on -- in the afternoon of the following day, but it was unsuccessful. It was repeated on the day after that in the morning, but with success that time. And the things that I mentioned occurred then, I mean the losses. And by midday, everything was clear except for a position east of Stolac for which I didn't have enough forces. At that moment, I was assisted by a unit commanded by Dragan Curcic of the HVO, who took that hill which -- which could threaten the town of Stolac, and a high-ranking officer from the command of the zone of operation was almost killed when my commanders came to inspect the situation. So I completely disagree with the -- with the statement that the Serbs walked away, and which can be corroborated that the very commander of the defence was killed in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, General, you entered Stolac with your troops. Was there a functioning civilian authority there which, until the beginning of the attack, took care of the -- of civilians at Stolac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No. When we entered Stolac, I have already said that the first attack was unsuccessful, so that the second wave of people who had fled Stolac turned up on the first evening after the unsuccessful attack, because it was clear that another attack would be -- would follow. The -- after two days of fighting, the Serbian population left the area with the troops, but the Serbs were a minority at Stolac. We didn't -- we hardly saw any Serbian civilians there once we entered. And the conditions had to be created for the return of the civilian population to Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We have minor problems with the transcript, so I would ask you, General, to repeat the part about the second wave of refugees. So what happened after the first unsuccessful attack?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: After the first unsuccessful attack, the representatives of the Muslim local authorities organised a group of civilians to leave Stolac and cross the confrontation line to the side that I controlled, and that second wave was also taken by buses away from the combat activities. On the following day -- what I just described happened during the night. And on the following day, in the morning, we attacked again, but this time with success. We took control of all most important positions around Stolac except for one. It was the detachment of -- called Bozan commanded by Dragan Curcic that actually took that position, and thus conditions were created to maintain defence positions and prepare for a counter-attack which was to be expected in the coming period. So Stolac was a vacated town, and around Stolac the forces of the HV and the HVO held their positions. The establishment of civilian authorities ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I was about to ask you about the establishment of civilian authorities. So you enter Stolac. There's no one. The only organised force is the army. You're in charge. And tell us, General, do you take any steps toward the establishment of civilian authorities at Stolac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: It was a joint effort in which I took part to organise life at Stolac, because there were indications that the population wanted to return to Stolac and the surrounding areas where they had their homes and land. There was also the wish of the persons who are -- or persons of esteem with both the Muslim and Croatian authorities who wanted to bring Stolac back to normal life.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately how much time elapsed since your entry into Stolac and the establishment of a body of civilian authority?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: For a few days there was intensive shelling from both sides, in parallel with some talks with the Serbian side about exchanging the dead bodies, but there were no conditions for civilian life, but about a week after the successful attack the civilians from the area -- it was both the civilians from the area and myself who launched this initiative to create the conditions for the refugees to return, and around about the 1st of July there was a meeting between the representatives of the Muslim and the Croatian communities where I put forward the military and security related situation, but I also demanded from them that they take upon them their responsibility, because there was an increasing pressure for the civilian population to return, which they should be enabled to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the testimony of a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a protective -- protected witness. Therefore, I ask the Trial Chamber to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, General, is it correct that at that meeting on the 1st of July it was agreed that a Crisis Staff be established that will be made up of 50 per cent Muslims and 50 per cent Croats and that it will discharge civilian authority?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct, and I believe that the witness described the very meeting that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The name Zeljko Raguz as president of that Crisis Staff, is it familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. He was the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Toward the end of 1992, Mr. Andjelko Markovic is mentioned as the person discharging civilian authority at Stolac. Do you have any knowledge about that or was it much later?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: I left the area in early August, so that must have been after my departure, and I have no knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you, General, to explain to the Trial Chamber whether or not a military unit was being established of -- and that consisted of the civilian population from Stolac. Do you know anything about it, and if so, did you play any role in it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. When I entered Stolac, I positioned a battalion to defend Stolac, which consisted to a great part of Croats from that area, and they carried out the attack in co-operation with the local Muslim leaders. Through the talks and conversations I had those days, it seemed to me very logical to make an offer to the Muslims' authority there, namely that younger Muslims should be included in the defence activities together with ethnic Croats. They accepted that. They invited young people to a place we had agreed on previously as sheltered from observation from the Serbian side, in the canyon of Bregava River, and over 400 people gathered there. I divided what used to be a battalion into two parts, and in every squad as the lowest-ranking unit, ten men strong, when I divided them - there was five people in each - and I placed in each squad five people of Muslim ethnicity, and thus I created two battalions of around 200 men each, with a 50/50 ratio in ethnic terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the commanding officers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: I accepted the Muslim share in leadership, but I placed two Croats in commanding positions. The commander of one battalion was Edin Obradovic, who had the required military skill and experience because he was a former JNA officer. And in the same way we found a few more people who had certain military skills and gave them appointments in those two newly established battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did Croat soldiers react, soldiers of Croat ethnicity, to your efforts to include Muslims into military units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Most of them accepted it, some with a certain amount of grumbling. A few were strongly opposed. Most of these defiant ones I managed to persuade from a military, human, ethical point of view, that it was the only fair solution, the only right one. And two men who no longer wanted to be part of this I sent away from the battalion and they were no longer members.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: These two that you sent away, they had been opposed to the creation of a joint Muslim-Croat army; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At that time, towards the end of June when all these operations had been finished, did you organise a meeting of representatives of military units, commanding officers, to see what to do next and compare notes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a meeting, a high-level meeting, in Grude, I believe - I'm not quite sure - attended by Mate Boban, a few more people from the Croatian government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. There was Mr. Petkovic. I can't remember the others, but those I named are certainly -- were certainly there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Petkovic give a speech then?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. He gave a cross-section of the situation from the military point of view, and he presented very frankly the problems we were facing. Surprisingly frankly, in my view. But I can say that I followed him with a great amount of understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P279 is going to be our next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to get back to what you've said, because this is important. You explained to us that there was fighting in Stolac, and in the month of August 1992, the Muslims had been placed on buses in order to protect them and they'd left the town. And then you took control of the town because the Serbs had been defeated. Therefore, at the time you enter Stolac, there are no Serbs left, there are no Muslims left, there are only the soldiers you are commanding. Was that exactly what the situation was like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were the only people there. There were no civilians there. It was an empty town. There was nothing to govern in an empty town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the 1991 census, the town of Stolac. I don't mean the municipality. I mean the town. There were recorded more than 5.000 inhabitants. So when you entered Stolac, there were no more Muslim civilians left. At that time, did Croats from the HVO tell you the Muslims must not come back. All we need to do is have a municipality that is solely inhabited by Croats, and then we can set up a Croatian brigade. Did people tell you this or did nobody mention this to you, and you on your own bat decided to set up these two battalions, one being a Croatian one, the other a Muslim one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if someone had told me that earlier or even at that time, I would have obviously gone against the orders or any such suggestion, because what I established there at that time, and I have to emphasise this, not a Muslim unit and a Croatian Army unit separated, but a joint army where each ethnicity was represented 50/50 at the level of every company and every battalion. It was mixed, 50/50, at every level. And I formed a Joint Command for these two battalions, and I called them the command of sector Stolac. And let me stress one more thing. At a point, that attempt that I had described earlier of establishing the BH Army, which had met with my understanding but eventually failed, these people now were also included in the joint forces of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What did you do to get the Muslim population back, those that had left on board the buses? Did you ask them to come back? What did you personally do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right after combat died down, I asked for a Crisis Staff to be set up, because that term was the easiest to use in the circumstances, because everyone knew what it meant and what the jurisdiction, the powers of a Crisis Staff are. I asked for that Crisis Staff, and both ethnic communities, Muslim and Croat alike, accepted it and accepted that it be mixed, 50/50. That's the way they set it up. From that moment on, they started rapidly assuming all the functions of civilian authority, organised the return of the population, protection of property, transportation, medical services, supply, and all the other aspects of restoring life to normal, relatively normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a while ago you said that you had captured some Serbs. What became of them? Did you imprison them? Were they exchanged? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My obligations as a commander were to turn over prisoners to the military police, and that's where my obligations ended. I really cannot tell you what happened with them after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you handed them over to the military police. The military police of the HVO, was it, or the military police of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was the HV, Croatian Army, police, because at that time the HVO did not have its police in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The Croatian politicians who were part of the crisis cell, well, were they reluctant to see Muslims alongside them? Were they happy about it? Did they find it a normal situation to have a 50/50 ratio or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The men who were initiated to become part of that Crisis Staff had that kind of personality that it was very likely they would accept it, and these people had authority among the population. But I also have to stress that on the Muslim side there was a wide variety of attitudes and thinking. And they also had to look for the right people for co-operation. And what I carried away from that meeting as my conclusion was that we did a good thing, that the best people had been chosen, and that this was -- had a good chance of success.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From what you know, did Croat and Muslim refugees then return to Stolac or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. At the time when I was there, for another 10 or so days, I noticed the first large groups of civilians coming back to Stolac and to their places around Stolac. I mean Muslims and Croats alike. Muslims even came back in greater numbers because they had not been long gone, and they had not had time to resettle in Croatia, whereas Croats had been refugees for a longer time and for all sorts of reasons. They needed more time to start returning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Registrar, let's move into private session, because I need to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just say that I acted the way we always acted whenever we wanted to quote a protected witness, private session, full name and surname. And when we wanted to use only initials, we did that in open session. I really tried very hard to do the right thing, and I'm sorry this -- I made an error.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, we are discussing the return of refugees. You told us Muslims were returning in larger numbers than Croats, and that leads me to my next question. At that time, did you ever notice that anyone in the military authorities or any one of the members of the Crisis Staff took any step whatsoever to prevent the Muslim refugees willing to return from coming back?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No. I never noticed anyone even thinking it, let alone doing something. And the return of refugees depended mostly on personal decisions of the people, but nobody did anyone [as interpreted] to prevent them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to that meeting we had mentioned and where you told us General Petkovic addressed it, although he wasn't a general then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document P279, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is a document we received from the Prosecution as the introductory statement of General Petkovic. We don't know where, at which meeting, and we do not know whether the words noted here had ever really been uttered. That's why I'm going to ask you, General Beneta, to the best of your recollection, at that meeting did Mr. Petkovic read from a paper or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: General Petkovic spoke. He spoke looking at his audience. I would say that he spoke from the heart. I think he was inspired in that speech, and he was saying the things that I believed, too, namely that in that area where I was with my unit of the Croatian Army, I was encountering the same problems that he was describing in his address.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At a meeting in June 1992, was it clear who the enemy was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Abundantly clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who was the enemy?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army and the armed forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask a question particularly regarding this. Mr. Petkovic sets out the tasks in four points. One is to put under control the remaining area of Croatian municipalities, and number four, to establish Croatian rule over all municipalities. Now, I do not quite see how this relates to the Serbs being the enemy. Doesn't it -- it not look as if there were a problem, at least, a problem also with the Muslims, with the non-Croats generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know where you drew that inference from when it is said: "Place under control the remaining territory of Croatian municipalities." Back then and today, still I understood that as an area populated by Croats in a percentage that is absolutely significant. I don't think he meant to say absolutely Croatian and turned against everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, one of the issues important to us now is whether what is stated here on paper was ever uttered at that meeting. So I'm asking you now. If I understood you correctly, then you said that General Petkovic at that meeting didn't read at all but looked at his audience and gave an inspired speech. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot say which percentage of this was actually said, but I can say that he spoke in an inspired manner looking at us, and I nodded in agreement several times because it seemed to me that he had hit the nail on the head as he was speaking. But whether he actually read out this entire text, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, at this meeting was there a proposition, implicit or explicit, in any manner, that the Muslims were the enemies of the Croats or that they would become their enemies one day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No. At that meeting, no such thing was said, and if it had been, it would not have been in accordance with the situation on the ground, because at those days, I actually established a unit consisting of Muslims and Croats at Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, tell us to whom did you hand over your military duties at Stolac before you left?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The sector of Stolac with the zone of responsibility and the forces defending that zone I handed over to the first brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Our next witness will continue speaking about this issue in relation to Stolac, and let us pass over to the next issue. The working title is "Operation South." This is our last topic, so we may actually finish your examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. General, I would like to remain on this document of June 26, 1992, before Stolac was taken by yourself. General Petkovic seems to be making a speech. At this document it's never mentioned that the enemy would be the Muslims. However, there is a strange sentence, item 4 where it says: "To establish Croatian rule over all municipalities." Municipalities which are not under HVO control, i.e., Mostar and Stolac." So according to you, what can this mean? To establish Croatian rule over these municipalities? What did he have in mind when he said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but which sentence are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on paragraph four, in the fourth paragraph. You have four bullet points, 1, 2, 3 and 4. I'm interested in bullet point number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The item: "To establish Croatian rule over all municipalities." That was going on in practice the way I explained. So one week after this was said, on the 1st of July a joint Staff of Croats and Muslims at Stolac was established, and it was partly my initiative. At that time, I took these words to mean the establishment of authority, and that authority at Stolac in all segments and in every aspect of its function was leaning on the Republic of Croatia. Not for political reasons, but there was no communication with anybody else. No truck with food or medicine for the population could have come from anywhere but from Croatia. So this language here I understood and implemented on the ground in the way that I have already described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with regard to this document, I would like us to state for the transcript that the Prosecution hasn't submitted any evidence that the text that we see before us on paper was ever uttered at any meeting. So we should keep this in mind. And General Petkovic, who signed this document, can certainly explain the meaning of any of its part, and I'm sure you will ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let us move to Operation South. To start with, tell us when that operation took place.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Operation South took place in mid-July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us whether that was really an operation in the sense as defined by the JNA doctrine, because we have heard of differences in the -- with regard to the notion of operation between the Yugoslav doctrine and the NATO doctrine.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes, there are such differences. In accordance with the doctrine that was known there at the time would not be considered an operation but, rather, a battle that took a very short time and small forces were involved. And under this definition of "operation," this doesn't qualify as one, but merely as a battle, as an attempt.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, where were you at the time in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Since the end of March of that year, I was transferred to the command of the military district of Split, and I was chief of anti-aircraft defence at a command. I dealt with -- I dealt with the issues related to the defence of the pontoon bridge near Zadar which was the only connection between the south and the north of Croatian at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, General, who sent you to participate in Operation South?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Mr. Dzanko, who at the time held the rank of colonel in the Croatian Army, and he was the deputy commander of the army district.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The verb is missing from this transcript. What did Mr. Dzanko do, did he ask you or order you, or what did he do?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: He asked me to take part.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, General.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Colonel Dzanko came to my observation point and asked me whether I was willing to accompany him to South-east Herzegovina, because an operation was to be staged there. I was in a position to refuse or accept to accompany him. I eventually accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The transcript read "He ordered me to take part." That's why we're repeating. Tell us, General, if you had refused that request, would you have suffered any detrimental consequences?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No. There would have been no detrimental consequences for me if I had refused.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, who was it that defined your task in that operation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: My task was defined by Mr. Dzanko at -- at the commander's reconnaissance that we carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did Mr. Dzanko define your task?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: In the introductory part when he was describing the military situation to me, he said that the Muslim forces were preparing to attack in the direction of the Neretva valley. When we say that, we mean the Neretva delta. That is Croatian territory, which leads to the town of Ploce, which is on the coast. He said that we must plan the operation, an attack operation, in which the 1st and the 3rd Brigades of the HVO would take part in the area south of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Should a part of the HVO's special unit Ludvig Pavlovic have taken part in the operation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Yes, it should have.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which area was to be liberated in that action?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: It was our task to liberate the area between the southern outskirts of Mostar up until Buna, which was controlled by Muslim forces. That should have been cut through, and thus the forces south of that area, that means around Blagaj, would have been cut off, and they would be forced to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to those plans, when was the operation to begin?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: It was to begin on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did it really start on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No, it did not, because in the night during -- or, rather, before the start of the operation which was to commence at dawn, considerable forces of the ABiH had moved through two -- two HVO brigades and attacked --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise, General. For the sake of the transcript, can you repeat the part about the forces of the ABiH that broke through? What --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: No, they didn't break through. They infiltrated. So without fighting. At night-time. They were able to move through the combat disposition of the defending forces without the defenders ever noticing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say "defenders," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: The forces of the 1st and 3rd Brigades of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. So they infiltrated. And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA
utterances.text: Fighting broke out behind those brigades, behind their positions, and there were killed and wounded soldiers on both sides. And it went on that night, the following day, and the following night. Only on the day that followed the first reports became available and it was possible to make the first analyses. Militarily, the situation was very complex.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my following questions refer to the statements made by the Prosecution witnesses about these actions, and I will have some documents about that that constitute a whole, so I believe now would be a logical time to break and start something new tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. As far as time is concerned, I think you have about 30 minutes left. The registrar will check. Altogether you had three hours at the beginning. I said there were to be about 30 minutes, not 13. Witness, you will come back tomorrow morning because we're sitting in the morning. Please be here for the 9.00 hearing tomorrow and make the necessary arrangements. Ms. Alaburic, you have used two hours and 24 minutes so far, so you have 36 minutes left. Thank you. I wish you all a pleasant evening. See you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
